newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - EU ministers say the die is cast for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU ministers say the die is cast for EMU.

text.p: European foreign ministers, celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome that created the European Union, said on Tuesday the bloc's single currency project marked another crucial watershed for Europe.
But doubts remained over the timing of the ambitious plan to replace at least some of the individual currencies of the 15 EU member nations with the euro from January 1 1999.
"The euro is a question of destiny for Europe, both internally and externally," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told reporters at the gathering in Rome.

Echoing the words of Julius Caesar on crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC to march on Rome, ministers from Germany and France made clear the die was cast for economic and monetary union (EMU) and there should be no stalling.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini suggested it might be in Europe's interests to postpone the start, saying that all EU countries were struggling to meet the stringent economic critieria for EMU aspirants, but he ruled out seeking a delay.
"We are all in a straightjacket," Dini said.
"Considering the evolution of our economies, an additional year would have been valuable for most countries...but Italy is not requesting a delay," he added.

French Foreign Minister Herve De Charette said his country would never suggest a delay to the planned start of EMU because that would require the impossible task of renegotiating the 1992 Maastricht Treaty that set out the framework for monetary union.
"France will never propose it," he said. "If you open a renegotiation...there will be no agreement at all on anything."
The launch of EMU is limited to countries which have met tough requirements laid down in the Treaty.

Financial markets have speculated that the start date could be put back because many countries, including Europe's economic powerhouse Germany, are showing signs that they might fail the test on the size of their 1997 budget deficits.
But Kinkel warned that a delay could bring disaster.
He said the value of the German mark would rise, leading to the loss of more jobs in Germany, and other currencies would also be devalued if EMU did not come.
"If we have problems on the jobs market at the moment, they would get a lot worse," Kinkel said, adding that global markets were anticipating that EMU would go ahead.

British Prime Minister John Major, campaigning in Britain ahead of the May 1 general election, warned that a botched EMU could lead to capital flowing into currencies such as sterling and the Swiss franc.
A revaluation of the mark would make German exports less competitive and risk increasing unemployment which, at 4.7 million, is at its highest since the 1930s.

In Germany, Chancellor Helmut Kohl insisted that EMU should start on schedule but added that it must not be at the expense of monetary stability. "The stability criteria of the Maastricht Treaty are not open to discussion," he said.

Rome is worried that the German authorities might seek to squeeze Italy, traditionally seen as politically unstable, out of the EMU starting line-up. But Dini issued a veiled threat to Italy's northern partners not to shut the south out.
"We shouldn't forget that the euro can't go ahead without the necessary votes," he said in an interview with newspaper Il Sole 24 Ore on Tuesday.
"The exclusion of Mediterranean countries together with, for example, Great Britain, could prevent the launch of EMU thanks to their negative votes."
